Science.summary: High in the central tower of Angkor Wat, an ancient Cambodian temple, paintings depict horseback riders and a traditional musical ensemble. Thousands of visitors pass these images daily without noticing them because they are faded to the point of invisibility.

Science.title: Researchers rewire ribosomes to specialize in one protein
Science.summary: Every cell relies on ribosomes, the molecular machines that read genetic instructions and use them to assemble proteins. A cell needs thousands of types of proteins at any one time, so ribosomes must be generalists, capable of using instructions to produce any protein.

Science.title: Ozempic and Wegovy may have an unexpected mental health benefit
Science.summary: Semaglutide, the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy, may have benefits that extend well beyond weight loss and diabetes. In a large Swedish study of nearly 15,000 people with bipolar disorder, its use was linked to a 21% lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization. Researchers think effects on inflammation and brain-related biological pathways could help stabilize mood, though other GLP-1 drugs did not show the same association.

Science.title: Fast radio bursts could help disentangle galactic feedback from dark matter effects
Science.summary: Intense, brief flashes of radio light called fast radio bursts (FRBs) travel across billions of light-years to reach Earth, passing through a fog of matter along the way. The bursts' origins are unclear but may originate from highly magnetized dead stars called magnetars. The denser the fog through which FRBs travel, the more dispersed their signals become—similar to the way a prism splits white light into a rainbow of colors.

Science.title: Sparse-data method estimates sea surface temperatures 40% more accurately than conventional approach
Science.summary: Researchers have developed a method for extrapolating sea surface temperatures from sparse data that is significantly more accurate than other commonly used computational methods and slightly more accurate than the best-performing AI model, while taking a fraction of the time to train. The work has implications for both short-term weather forecasting and longer-term climate predictions.

Science.title: Early statin use linked to 15% lower dementia risk
Science.summary: Starting statins soon after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis may do more than protect the heart. In a nationwide Danish study of more than 132,000 people, those who began statin treatment within a year of diagnosis had a 15% lower relative risk of developing dementia over 10 years compared with those who did not start statins.

Science.title: Optimizing tomato plant growth with microbes
Science.summary: Plants are home to a diverse array of microorganisms that support their growth and help them adapt to environmental stress—of which there has been an abundance lately. High temperatures and drought caused by human-induced climate change have led to reduced crop yields and the use of biofertilizers such as rhizosphere microorganisms, which help plants absorb nutrients and increase their resistance to disease and stress.

Science.title: Google scientists removed a critical 'consciousness safeguard' from AI models. What happened next?
Science.summary: A new study shows that measures to stop AI's claims of consciousness have unintended consequences for non-human entities.

Science.title: Scientists observe Einstein’s gravity in the quantum world for the first time
Science.summary: Physicists have directly observed a long-predicted quantum effect of gravity, putting one of Einstein’s foundational ideas to a striking new test. Using ultracold atoms, researchers split an atom’s quantum wave so that one part was held in place while the other fell freely under gravity, then reunited the two to measure the tiny difference that emerged.

Science.title: Waterlogged seeds reveal melons' ancient journey
Science.summary: Melons produce many seeds, making the melon shape a traditional symbol of fertility and prosperity in Chinese culture. But the historical debate about how melons made their way to modern tables is as long and twisted as the vines they grow on.

Science.title: Action on climate and air pollution likely to boost economy, UN says
Science.summary: Every US$1 invested in tackling climate change and air pollution together can generate around US$15 in economic benefits, according to a report published today by the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC).

Science.title: Searching for unknown fungi in the Norwegian mountains
Science.summary: During some days in August, science takes center stage. The experts are surveying the little-known diversity of fungi found in the alpine Dryas heath. They may even discover species that have never been described scientifically before.

Science.title: Helium-3 lifts new quantum computing concept with faster tunneling rates
Science.summary: Helium—the lightest atom that can be laser-cooled and controlled—powers a new design for high-powered, stable quantum computers.

Science.title: Why does microwaving fish smell so bad?
Science.summary: The work break room can be a place of rest, gossip, fun or recovery. But it can also be a cause for complaint when yesterday's fish dinner becomes a smelly microwaved lunch. For most people, microwaving fish at work is a big no-no. It has even led to armed confrontations.

Science.summary: We can all see the huge waste of talent this represents for the young people concerned and society as a whole.

Science.title: Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 08 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02497-2 Strengthened laws should help to ensure future deaths are quickly disclosed to the public, but China’s reputation for such research is at risk.

Science.title: Germany's 15-year-olds post lowest PISA results since testing began 25 years ago
Science.summary: The PISA study regularly assesses 15-year-olds' ability to understand and solve real-life problems in reading, mathematics and science toward the end of their compulsory education. It demonstrates the extent to which young people are prepared for the demands of a knowledge-based society and can participate in social life on their own terms.

Science.title: The American “cheetah” wasn’t a cheetah at all
Science.summary: The extinct “American cheetah” was not really a cheetah at all, but a puma relative with an unexpectedly flexible lifestyle. Fossils from the Yukon suggest northern populations survived partly by eating fish, possibly including salmon, while southern cats hunted on land.

Science.title: Astrophotographer captures jaw-dropping view of the Crescent Nebula
Science.summary: Astrophotographer Kevin Boardman spent more than 16 hours capturing the intricate filaments of the Crescent Nebula.

Science.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized
Science.summary: More than 1,200 genetic variants have been linked to the Big Five personality traits, and many of the same variants are also associated with health, longevity, careers, income, and everyday habits. The findings reveal a surprisingly wide genetic connection between personality and life outcomes while showing that environment still plays a powerful role.

Science.title: Where on Earth is safest from global catastrophe?
Science.summary: Researchers have worked out the safest, most resilient country to be in during an apocalyptic event.

Science.title: Arctic warming fuels 2 distinct climate regimes in Siberia that could wake up a methane 'sleeping giant'
Science.summary: New research finds that western Siberia is becoming wetter as the world warms, while eastern Siberia seems to be getting drier. And both these conditions are fueling a rise in methane emissions, spelling trouble for the climate.

Science.title: Curved nanographene with five-, six- and seven-membered rings synthesized in two steps
Science.summary: Nanographenes can be considered molecular fragments of graphene, a 2D conductive material in which carbon atoms are connected in a honeycomb pattern. Because their electronic and photophysical properties vary depending on the size and shape of the molecule, nanographenes are expected to find applications in OLEDs, organic solar cells, organic field-effect transistors and more.

Science.title: Doctors saved this rare monkey from amputation. Months later, she gave birth
Science.summary: A critically endangered roloway monkey has given birth just months after surgeons performed an unusual operation that saved her foot from amputation. Her new daughter, Lagertha, is an important addition to a species believed to number fewer than 2,000 in the wild.

Science.title: Eerily humanlike AI-powered robot enters mass production in China — its makers say it could soon be helping you out at home
Science.summary: Xpeng's engineers have designed a humanoid robot that they say is the first in the world that will walk itself off the production line.

Science.title: When disaster strikes, what happens to our pets?
Science.summary: As large-scale disasters—including earthquakes, torrential rains, typhoons and wildfires—become increasingly frequent, ensuring that pets as well as their owners can evacuate safely and receive appropriate care has become an important part of disaster preparedness.

Science.title: Grandchildren repay childhood care by supporting ailing grandparents in Hong Kong
Science.summary: As Hong Kong Special Administrative Region's population ages at one of the fastest rates in the world, demand for family elder care increases daily. To understand the responsibilities and roles assumed by grandchildren in caring for their grandparents, the Asia-Pacific Institute of Aging Studies (APIAS) at Lingnan University conducted an in-depth interview study.

Science.title: Portugal's Pinhal Interior shows why fire and floods are part of the same cycle
Science.summary: Across southern Europe, increasingly extreme heat, wildfire and intense rainfall are forcing planners to consider how one event can alter the risk of the next. Portugal's exceptionally wet winter and another summer of wildfire risk are an example of this. As a professor of architecture and climate change adaptation who has been following the cyclical nature of weather extremes in the Pinhal Interior region since the deadly 2017 fires, I explain why prevention must connect forests, settlements, slopes and waterways.

Science.title: Did wildfires help spark the invention of pottery?
Science.summary: A new study suggests that a period of intense fires and landscape upheaval in the ancient southern Levant may have helped create the conditions that led Neolithic communities to discover how fire could transform clay.

Science.title: From classrooms to careers, Black women describe lasting effects of racialized bias
Science.summary: As a child, Nefatari excelled at advanced mathematics. But a teacher questioned her academic success in this area because the teacher believed Black girls were not good at math. Years later, as a research participant, Nefatari said the teacher's influence steered her away from her preferred field.

Science.summary: Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) scientists used simulations to understand the role disruptive impacts play on icy moons with subsurface oceans in our solar system. A recent paper published in the journal Nature Astronomy concludes that disruptive impacts can affect the presence and persistence of subsurface oceans in these moons but do not seem to create new oceans.
